<!-- Purpose: index the executable TypeScript surface and its boundary contracts.
Open Obligations: None. -->
# MeTTa in TypeScript

> The engine runs inside your Node process, on a WebAssembly SWI-Prolog. No
> system SWI, no Python, no separate server. This file is how to USE the seat;
> the repository root's llms.txt covers the language and every other surface.

## Install

```sh
npm ci --prefix extensions/node
```

That fetches the compiler and test tooling and builds the TypeScript, the
browser bundle and the engine copy the package mounts, through the package's
own `prepare` script, so a checkout that has run it carries dist/, browser/ and
_runtime/. Node 22.18 or newer, which is what package.json declares. `prepare`
rather than `prepack` because it is the one script npm's directory fetcher
runs, so `npm install file:/path/to/extensions/node` gets a package with the
engine in it.

## The host

The engine runs on a patched WebAssembly SWI-Prolog this package carries in
`_host/`: `swipl-web.cjs`, emscripten's loader, beside `swipl-web.wasm` and
`swipl-web.data`, the data image holding SWI's library and, at
/swipl/metta-host.pl inside it, the declaration of the patches the build
carries. It is SWI-Prolog 10.1.14 with every patch in MesTTo/MeTTa's
`tests/checks/host_workarounds/` applied, compiled by npm-swipl-wasm's own
recipe through that repository's `tools/wasm-host/build.sh`. Node requires the
loader from `_host/`; the browser build bundles it and fetches the other two
from `_runtime/wasm/`.

Every boot runs the engine's host check before the engine loads. A host that
does not declare every required patch, npm's `swipl-wasm` among them, is
refused with `EngineError` (`ERR_METTA_ENGINE`) carrying the engine's own
sentence, which names each missing patch, and nothing reaches the console.

## First call

```ts
import { metta, S, V, fn } from "./extensions/node/src/index.ts";

const m = await metta();
await m.eval(fn.add(1, 2)).one();     // 3
```

## Building terms

`S` makes symbols and expressions, `V` makes variables, `fn` names the
engine's own operations. A call on `S` is an expression with that head, and
the head is exactly the symbol you wrote:

```ts
S.parent(S.alice, S.bob)      // (parent alice bob)
V.x                           // $x
fn.add(1, 2)                  // (+ 1 2), which reduces to 3
S.add(1, 2)                   // (add 1 2), a term with no meaning attached
```

That last pair is the one to get right. `fn` maps a readable name onto the
operation the engine actually has, so `fn.add` is `+`; `S.add` builds a term
headed by the symbol `add`, which nothing defines, so it comes back unreduced.

The free word functions are the same words: `add`, `gte`, `If` and the rest
build their head's expression when called, and where a term goes each IS its
head, so `typed(S.plus, add)` is `(: plus +)` and `m.fn.getType(add)` asks
about `+`; each used to cross as an opaque host value. A call is not a word:
`S.f(x)` builds the call and a defined `f(x)` asks it, so an ask, or a promise
nobody awaited, where a term goes raises `NameError` naming both remedies,
where it used to cross as a live JavaScript object nothing reads.

A gap stands for a RUN of children: `seg(V.rest)` is `(:seg $rest)`, whose
match answers the run it took as one expression, and `seg()` is the anonymous
gap `...`, each occurrence its own, so `S.order(seg())` matches an `order` of
any arity.

A number crosses as its kind: a safe integer as a `number` and a wider one as
a `bigint`, a float as a `number` in a `FloatAtom` (`float(2)` is 2.0), and a
rational as the exact `Rational` in a `RationalAtom`, printing `1r3`, where it
used to refuse. `G(new Rational(1n, 3n))` makes one. The portable transport
refuses a rational, having no tag for one.

A type position (`arrow`, `typed`, and `{ type }` on `define` and `state`)
reads host types through `typeAtom`: a term is itself, an array is an
expression type (`[S.List, Number]` is `(List Number)`), a JavaScript
constructor names the type the engine admits its values at (`Number` and
`BigInt` are `Number`, `String` is `String`, `Boolean` is `Bool`, `Object` is
`Atom`, `Array` is `Expression`), an atom class names its metatype (`Sym` is
`Symbol`, `Var` is `Variable`), `Space` and `SpaceHandle` are `SpaceType`, and
any other class names what `registerType` taught it or its base, else its own
name. A function that is no class raises `NameError`; it used to cross as an
opaque host value, so `arrow(Number, Number)` built
`(-> (js Function) (js Function))`. `arrow` takes any number of positions, so
a nullary operation's type is its result alone: `arrow(Number)` is
`(-> Number)`, as the engine declares `current-time`.

A value only the engine can hold, a C blob such as `re-compile`'s pattern or
`database-open!`'s store, crosses as a `NativeHandle`, a Grounded atom that is
its own host value: the engine keeps it in a registry and this side holds the
id (`handle.ident`), so handing it back reaches the very same value and the
same value crossing again is the same atom. `handle.release()` or leaving a
`using` block lets the engine drop it, and so does collecting the last atom
naming it, either with the engine's next crossing; a released handle, or one
from another engine, is refused wherever it is sent, and the portable
transport refuses every handle as it refuses a live host value. It used to
raise `metta_node_untaggable` at the boundary.

## A lowered body

`m.define(function f(...) {...})` reads a plain function's own source and
installs ONE equation. Inside it: arithmetic, comparisons, the bitwise
operators (`&` `|` `^` `~` `<<` `>>` are `bit-and` and its family, over
unbounded integers; `>>>` refuses), `&&` and `||` (short-circuiting, so
`and-then` and `or-else`; the relational `and`/`or` are the words `and(a, b)`
and `or(a, b)`), `if`, ternaries,
`const` (a `let`; a run of them is `let*`), `const [a, [b, c]] = v` (a
pattern `let`), `switch` (a `case`, `default` tried last), a statement run for
its effect (`chain`), a bare `return;` or running off the end (the unit `()`)
and recursion. `this` is the space the definition installs into:
`this.match(p, t)` and `this.atoms()` lower to `match` and `get-atoms`, and a
write names its head, `fn.addAtom(this, x)`; a parameter declared as a
`Space` and a space from `{ scope }` take the same two methods. A structural
case is `caseOf(x).with(pattern, ({ a }) => ...).otherwise(() => ...)` (or
`.end()` for no catch-all), each handler destructuring its pattern's
variables; `_` is the anonymous variable. Atoms are mentioned as they are
built: `S.name`, `S.f(a, b)`, `S["x"]`, `S("exact")`, `V.x`, `fn.carAtom(x)`,
`G("text")`, `float(2)`. Word-door functions (`If`, `Let`, `Collapse`,
`Superpose`, `Quote`, `Empty`, `Match`, `carAtom`, `neg`, `e`, `nil`, the
operator words) and constants (`TRUE`, `FALSE`, `UNIT`, `UNDEFINED`) are read
by their exported names after the engine's own heads. Another definition is
called by the name its function was written with, `isIn(x, xs)` reaching the
head `in` that `{ name: "in" }` installed; a name two definitions share
refuses. What `define` returns is its head in term position, so `h(twice, 2)`
passes the symbol and `G(twice)` the live object. A generator body is
TRACED instead, which is the door for queries (`yield* m.match(...)`).
An array's `map`, `filter` and `reduce` in a body are `map-atom`,
`filter-atom` and `foldl-atom` (an arrow callback is the template, a named
function the function form; `reduce` needs its initial value).
An arrow function in a body is a lambda, `(v) => v < k` being
`(|-> ($v) (< $v $k))` (a binder shadowing a body name is renamed fresh), and
`m.lambda(arrow)` lowers one from host code into the term, applied as
`m.eval([lam, 21])`.
`Math`'s functions keep their JavaScript meaning on the engine's math heads:
`Math.abs(x)` is `(abs-math x)`, and so `acos` `asin` `atan` `ceil` `cos`
`exp` `floor` `pow` `sin` `sqrt` `tan` `trunc`; `Math.log(x)` is
`(log-math e x)`; `Math.round` rounds a tie up, where `round-math` rounds it
away from zero; `Math.max` and `Math.min` fold `max` and `min`. `Math.PI`,
`Infinity` and `NaN` are their numbers. Any other Math function refuses, and
one handed to `map`, `filter` or `reduce` must take what the walk passes.
Equations whose HEADS are patterns go through `m.rules(function* name(x, xs)
{ yield rewrite(S.f(S.leaf), 0); ... })`: the generator runs once with its
parameters as variables and every yield, which must be an equation, is stored
as written; a goal or a non-equation refuses before anything lands.

## Asking the engine's functions, and importing

`m.fn.carAtom(x)` ASKS `(car-atom x)` where `fn.carAtom(x)` only builds it;
`kb.fn` asks in `kb`, and `m.fn("exact-head")` is the exact door.
`m.import(lib.spaces)` is `(import! &self (library lib_spaces))`;
`lib("name")`, `lib("alias", "file")` and a host path string are the other
module forms, and `kb.import(...)` imports into `kb`.

Under Node the engine sees this host's files at their own paths and starts in
this process's working directory: every top-level directory is mounted live
through NODEFS except the engine's own `/dev`, `/proc`, `/swipl` and `/metta`,
a Windows drive is `/c` and so on, and `tmp_dir` is a directory of the
engine's own inside the one a native SWI-Prolog here would choose, TMP or else
`/tmp` (TEMP on Windows), removed by `dispose()`. So `loadFile`,
`libraryPath` and a host path given to `import` read the file where it is, and
a relative path in a program resolves as it does for the native engine; they
used to copy the file's directory into the engine's own filesystem, which a
relative path never reached. `m.engine.mount(dir, "/data")` shows a host
directory at another engine path, live.

## Asking, lazily

An answer set is a whole Promise of its answers (`then`, `catch`, `finally`)
and nothing runs until you await it, so `assert.rejects(ans, ErrorClass)` and
`Promise.all([...])` take it directly:

```ts
const ans   = m.match(S.parent(V.x, S.bob));   // nothing has run yet
const rows  = await ans;                        // the whole answer set
const who   = await ans.one();                  // exactly one, or a refusal
const maybe = (await ans.find()) ?? S.none;     // at most one, so ?? composes
```

Abandoning an answer set stops the work: taking two rows of two thousand costs
two rows.

## Bounding and cancelling

```ts
await m.eval(term).until(AbortSignal.timeout(50));
```

## What a refusal is

The engine says which refusal it raised and this seat raises that class, so a
caller never matches the message. One class per kind the engine publishes:
`syntax` (`MettaSyntaxError.line`), `time_limit` and `inference_limit`
(`TimeLimitError.limit`, `InferenceLimitError.limit`), `restraint`
(`RestraintError.restraint`, `.limit`, `.call`), `interrupted`
(`InterruptedError`), `value` and `type` (`WireError`, `CastError`),
`assertion` (`AssertionError.operation`, and as atoms `.actual`, `.expected`,
`.missing` and `.excess`), `capability`
(`CapabilityError.space`, `.operation`, `.capability`), `platform`
(`PlatformCapabilityError.requires`, `.costs`, and the operation and
capability it inherits), `operation`
(`OperationError.operation`, `.kind`, `.expected`, `.culprit`), `stack`
(`StackLimitError.limit`) and `source` (`SourceNotFoundError.source`); anything
else is `EngineError`. A `limit` is `undefined` where a budget expired inside a
nested query, which is the one case the engine cannot name the number. The list
is `tests/data/error-kinds.json`, shared with the Python seat.

A host operation's failure is the value it threw. A `MettaError` is raised at
the outer call as itself. Anything else, thrown, rejected or raised by a
generator midway, is the `cause` of the `EngineError` raised there. MeTTa code
that catches the failure reads `(metta_node_host_error Message Key)` inside
its `Error`, where `Key` names the thrown value until the job closes.

Every refusal also carries `.ground` and `.remedy`, read off the engine's own
`(refusal ...)` catalog row for its kind and rendered by the engine with this
refusal's own fields in it: `error.remedy.title` is one line saying what to do
(`raise the bound past 0.05 seconds, or narrow the query`), `.applicability` is
rustc's (`machine`, `maybe`, `prose`) and `.edit` is the MeTTa to write, as
source text for `m.parse`. `.ground.kind` is `metta-law` or `arbiter` and
`.citation` names the place. `toJSON()` carries both, so a structured log keeps
them. `website/reference/refusals.md` is the whole table.

```ts
try { m.run("!(collapse (upto 10))"); }        // (cache upto (max-answers 2))
catch (e) {
  if (e instanceof RestraintError) console.log(e.restraint, e.limit, e.call);
}
```

A failed assertion hands a harness its parts as ATOMS, read off the refusal by
the engine's own classifier: `.actual` is what a `test` produced or an
`assert`'s goal, `.expected` what the source asked for, and `.missing` and
`.excess` the answers a bag comparison found absent and extra. A part the form
does not carry is `undefined`, which differs from the empty bag: two empty bags
say the answers agree and differ only in order.

## Spaces

```ts
const kb = m.space(S.kb);
using temporary = m.space(); // anonymous native space, released at block exit
```

A space can be created with restricted grants, and ordinary computation still
runs inside one that has none:

```ts
const locked = m.space(S.locked, { grants: [] });
await locked.eval(S.double(21)).one();        // 42
const reader = m.space(S.reader, { grants: ["file"] });
```

Space and State objects implement `ATOM_OF`: pass them directly in terms.
Released spaces refuse operations, including queries first consumed after
release. A new `m.space(name)` opens a new handle after the old one is released.

## Joins, guards, prepared queries and temporary facts

```ts
const adults = kb.prepare(S[","](S.person(V.name), S.age(V.name, V.age)), {
  where: fn.gte(V.age, 18), limit: 10,
});
adults.columns;                  // ["name", "age"]
adults.term;                     // the query's native term
await adults.solve();            // current answers, never a cached result
await adults.solve({ given: [S.person(S.ada), S.age(S.ada, 36)] });
```

`kb.match(pattern, { where, limit })` is the immediate form. Join with `S[","]`;
the engine unifies shared variables. `where` is a native boolean term, lowered
as `(let true guard template)` inside the match. `limit` wraps it in `(take n ...)`
and must be a positive safe integer. Both survive tracing through `yield*`.
An evaluated template remains the second positional argument; wrap ordinary
host objects with `G` so they cannot be mistaken for an options object.

Preparation caches the term, wire and columns, with no cursor until a solve is
consumed. `solve({ signal })` cancels one execution. `solve({ given })` names
`kb.withFacts(given, adults.term)`: add facts and evaluate the term inside an
engine snapshot, discarding **all** writes on exit. It preserves existing equal
occurrences and their tokens. This closed computation cannot yield to a host
callback; an ordinary solve can. An assumption scope spanning arbitrary
JavaScript needs a shared exact-occurrence-removal service and is not exposed.

## Transactions and speculation

`kb.transaction(term)` is `(transaction term)`, returning every answer;
`kb.speculate(term)` evaluates under an engine snapshot and discards writes.
`m.transaction` and `m.speculate` target `m.self`. Their bodies are native terms,
not JavaScript callbacks: `engine_yield/1` cannot cross those SWI query frames.

`using policy = m.atomic()` applies a transaction to **each call** until
disposal; `m.speculative()` applies a snapshot to each call. Space methods of
the same names install the same engine-wide policies. Several calls in a
JavaScript block do not form a transaction. Build one native term for that.
Do not keep an ambient policy across unrelated concurrent host work.

## Reified worlds

`m.world(space)` is the existing mutable draft with atomic delta commit and
explicit restore. It is not a reified world. Reification, successor evaluation,
diff and conflict-checked commit currently live in Python's binding; the shared
engine publishes no complete service for them. There is no TypeScript `reify`
door. The remedy is a shared engine service, not a second host world model.

## Mutable cells

```ts
const balance = m.state(10, { type: S.Number });
balance.set(12).held;                          // 12
String(await m.eval(fn.getState(balance)).one()); // "12"
```

The cell carries its native handle. `fn["change-state!"]` is the exact engine
head, while `.set` follows the JavaScript collection convention and returns
the cell. The engine checks its declared `StateMonad` type.

## Spaces implemented in TypeScript

The engine queries your own data. A `Map`, an array, a `Set` or a plain object
attaches as a live view in one line; anything with a shape of its own
implements `SpaceProvider` and only the methods its backend has.

```ts
const rows = new Map([["ada", 3]]);
const scores = m.attach("&scores", rows);      // live: no publication step
await scores.match(S.kv(V.who, V.n));

m.attach("&table", {
  *match(pattern) { /* yield CANDIDATES; the engine unifies */ },
  add(atom) { ... },
});
```

Capabilities are derived from the methods present, so what a provider cannot do
is refused by name. `tsmetta/spaces` composes them: `union`, `readOnly`,
`overlay`, `mapped`, `diff`, `objectView`.

## Proofs, and asking the engine about itself

```ts
String(await m.why(S.quad(3)));   // the first proof, rendered
m.derivation(target);             // every proof, as a discriminated union
m.doc(S.area);                    // the (@doc ...) atom
m.solve(4, sub(V.x, 1));          // { x: 5 }: the relation, backwards
m.cast(S.Ann, S.Person);          // narrowed, or CastError naming its real types
m.forms(source);                  // every top-level form, read and not run
m.trace("!(quad 3)");             // the engine's own call and exit events
m.disassemble("dbl");             // the clauses the name compiled to
m.evalStatus(S.Point(1, 2));      // value, not-reducible or empty, for a TERM
m.reducible(S.Point(1, 2));       // false: nothing applies to that head
using _ = m.strict();             // refuse anything answered unreduced, both doors
using _ = m.limits({ inferences: 100_000 });
```

A term is as deep as the ENGINE can hold: nothing on this side recurses per
nesting level, `m.parse` answers at 500,000 deep, and past the engine's own
stack the refusal is `StackLimitError` carrying the ceiling in bytes. That
ceiling is `m.engine.stackLimit`. With no `METTA_STACK_LIMIT`, boot sets it
once the engine has loaded to half of what the host's memory can still grow
to, about 2 GiB on this build, so the heap holds the stacks at the ceiling
and SWI's own refusal comes before the heap runs out. `METTA_STACK_LIMIT`, or
`config.configure({ stackLimit })` before the first boot, replaces it in either
direction; the variable is read as every seat reads it, decimal digits alone,
and above the derived ceiling a heap that runs out first answers the engine's
`no_memory` error instead.
`m.dispose()` releases the surface and every door refuses with `ClosedError`
afterwards, including an ask that was in flight.

## Standing queries

```ts
using watch = subscribe(kb, S.alarm(V.what), { onEvent: (e) => log(e) });
using view = await LiveView.open(kb, S.alarm(V.what));
```

Subscriptions honor their caller's `signal`. Breaking an async iteration ends
that subscription; queue overflow is a refusal with a remedy. `publish` is an
ordinary space write and `fold` accumulates host state over the admission stream.
`kb.reacts` and `kb.agenda` publish engine reaction and ordering declarations.

## Materialized answers

```ts
using joined = kb.live(S.person(V.name), S.age(V.name, V.age));
joined.rows;                         // readonly binding rows
joined.count({ name: S.ada, age: 36 }); // occurrence multiplicity
for await (const delta of joined.changes({ signal })) {
  // add/remove carry a row; progress marks a complete committed generation
}
```

The engine seeds and registers a live query atomically and recomputes after
committed segments. Each change consumer has its own bounded queue. Rollback
and speculation emit no changes. Closing retains the final snapshot.
`LiveView` uses this same native multiset, so opening races and variable-pattern
removals cannot leave stale counts. This recomputes the native query; it does
not promise incremental join maintenance.

`kb.liveEval(call)` requires a private incremental tabled definition, declared
with `(cache head (incremental private))` in the catalog. Shared tables and
queries that would yield to host code are refused at the snapshot boundary.
`kb.effectPlan(term)` returns the engine's transitive operation/effect analysis
without running the term.

## Coordination

`race`, `merge`, `parMap`, `every`, `Channel`, `spawn`: the platform's own
concurrency, each taking an `AbortSignal`. The engine's `library(thread)` is
absent from a WebAssembly build, so this is where concurrency lives.

Each `MeTTa` owns an engine. Dispose its dependent resources before disposing
it. Async host I/O can overlap; pure reductions use one WebAssembly engine.
Independent workers need independent engines and exchange portable wire atoms.
Abort signals act at answer boundaries; an inference budget bounds a reduction
that does not reach one promptly.

## The satellites

The root carries what a program reaches for. Everything else is in the package's
subpaths and costs nothing unimported: `tsmetta/ambient` (a lazily booted
default engine), `/spaces`, `/structures` (`AlphaSet`, `PatternMap`,
`MatchIndex`, `ClosureView`, `TabledMap`), `/matching` (unification and alpha
keys, no engine needed), `/testing` (generators and a shrinking property
runner), `/vocabularies` (the engine's closed value sets, checked against
`&metta`), `/strategies`, `/paths`, `/parallel`, `/subscribe`, `/derivation`,
`/provider`, `/wire`, `/convert`, `/integrate`, `/algebra`, `/remote`,
`/arrays`, `/tables`, `/tokens`, `/saga`, `/lint`, `/manifest`, `/events`,
`/config`, `/random`, `/version`, `/live`. README.md lists every exported
subpath and its test checks that list against package.json.

## Arrays, tables and native algebras

A shared table, the default, outlives the evaluation that built it: every ask
of the instance reads it, and `(table-stats ...)` reads its counters from any
later ask. A private table belongs to the engine that fills it. Every
synchronous ask (`run`, `runOne`, `load`, the space doors) runs in one engine
the instance keeps, as the Python seat's eager runs do, so a private table and
exact memoization, which keeps a private table, outlive a synchronous ask. An
awaiting ask (`eval`, a stream) runs in an engine of its own, so what it keeps
privately lasts that ask: read those counters before its answer stream closes.
Bounded memoization keeps its entries across every ask.

`tsmetta/arrays` uses `TypedArray` storage. `new Tensor(data, shape)` validates
nonnegative safe-integer dimensions and the element count, publishes `(Tensor dtype dimensions...)` as `.type`, and
reshapes by sharing storage. `installArrays(m)` registers the array operations;
`EmbeddingStore` supplies a vector-neighbour provider. No numeric library is
named by core.

`tsmetta/tables` maps record arrays or a `TableSource` into atoms.
`bridge(S.person(V.name, V.age), "people", {name: V.name, age: V.age})`
declares the row mapping; `tableSpace(source, declarations)` makes the provider.
`arrayTables({people: rows})` is the in-memory source. A database integration
implements `rows(table, constraints)` using its own parameterized SQL driver.
Repeated bridge variables must agree across columns. Literal dollar signs remain
ordinary filter values. Awaiting a truncated query also awaits provider cleanup.
There is no pandas adapter or SQL dialect translator in core.

`matchUnder(space, pattern, carrier)` from `tsmetta/algebra` names the native
`(match-under space carrier pattern)` and streams `{value, tag}` atoms.
`taggedFact` and `taggedRule` build its data. `counting` counts proofs, `prob`
combines weights, `S.product(...)` combines carriers and `S.formula(S.prob)`
accounts for overlapping proofs. The engine owns the fixpoint and laws.
Pass a carrier name or term; a host `Algebra` object raises
`AlgebraDeclarationError`.

## Remote serving and application doors

`tsmetta/remote` supplies `serve({spaces, port, token})`, an HTTP gateway with
an explicit space allow-list, loopback default and optional required bearer
token. Own it with `await using`. `connect(url, {space, token})` is a provider
to attach to another runtime. Cursor pulls stay lazy and structured errors
cross the wire; live JavaScript references do not.

HTTP application routes and GraphQL resolvers await queries and project rows.
Their schema, framework and authorization policy belong to the application or
an extension package, so core has no GraphQL schema generator or framework
integration roster.

## Crossing a host type, and a value that owns its matching

```ts
import { registerType } from "tsmetta/convert";
registerType(Person, {
  name: "Person",
  toAtom: (p) => [p.name, p.age],
  fromAtom: (name: string, age: number) => new Person(name, age),
});
// project(new Person("Ada", 36))  ->  (Person "Ada" 36)
```

A registration picks one of four images, and the four are the engine's own
`registry-image` vocabulary: `expression` (the default shaped form), `symbol`
(a bare name, which is how an enum reads, and it runs backwards too), `handle`
and `operations` (by reference). `autoImage(value)` is the rung beneath a
declared image and answers `"transparent"` or `"opaque"` in constant time; an
iterator is always opaque, because measuring one drains it.

A host value can also decide what it unifies with, which is Hyperon's
`CustomMatch`: give the class a `[CUSTOM_MATCH](other)` method and call
`registerCustomMatch(m.engine, TheClass)`. Registration is what turns the seam
on, so a program that does not use it carries no clause for it at all.

## Extending this seat: one declared table of points

`tsmetta/seam` is this seat's extension seam, the seat-level twin of
`engine/ext_points.pl`. A point is DECLARED with a kind and its fields, a
registrant is a ROW against one, and both read back as data:
`seam.declared()`, `seam.rows()`, `seam.at(name)`. Four kinds, the engine's own
less the `host_service` split a seat has no audience for: `declaration` (every
row read), `ownership` (the first row whose `claims(...)` answers wins),
`event` (every row's `on(...)` runs), `service` (the seat writes it, a
registrant calls it). `<point>.table()`, `.claim(...)`, `.each(...)` and
`.call()` dispatch by kind and refuse the other kinds' spelling;
`.register(name, { ...fields })` refuses an undeclared point, a missing field
or an extra one by name; `.refusal(subject)` is the sentence a caller gets when
no row answers, naming the door and the registrants there are.

Points: `type`, `repr` and `reflector` keep the storage `registerType`,
`registerRepr` and `registerReflector` always used and are declared here so the
surface is one query; `provider`, `library` and `integration` are what packages
advertise under the `spaces`, `libraries` and `integrations` groups, read
UNLOADED. Services: `term`, `name`. `seam.point(name, kind, {fields, doc})`
declares one of your own. `seam.publish(surface)` writes the table into
`&metta` under `(kind extension-point ...)` and `(kind extension ...)`.

A package advertises registrations under a fourth group, `extensions`, in its
`package.json` `metta` field; `seam.advertised()` answers the names without
importing anything and `await seam.discover()` loads them. Loading is explicit
rather than on first dispatch because ESM `import()` is asynchronous; a package
that registers from its own module body needs neither call.

`tsmetta/seam` is a Node-only subpath, beside `tsmetta/integrate` and for
its reason: it reads a `package.json`, which a browser page has neither of.

This seat declares NO `frame` point and NO `array` point: it has no frame
notion, and its array notion is the platform's own `TypedArray` family, which
every numeric library in this runtime already produces. It names no third-party
library anywhere; the SWI-Prolog it runs the engine on is its own build in
`_host/` and `acorn` is the parser its `define` lowering uses.

## Integrating a library

`tsmetta/integrate` wraps a module, an object or one function as operations,
installs atomically, and discovers packages that advertise themselves in their
own `package.json` under `metta.integrations`, `metta.spaces` or
`metta.libraries`. `entryPoints(group)` answers advertised names without
importing anything; `discover()` returns integrations in install order and
refuses a requirement cycle. `installReflectionOps(m)` adds `(js-attr $o $n)`
and the two-mode relation `(js-field $o $n)`, which answers a `(name value)`
pair whether the name arrives bound or unbound.

## What a space declares, and a notation of your own

`kb.handles(pattern, "Exact" | "Partial" | "Sound" | "Refuse")` declares how
faithfully a space answers one query shape, keyed by shape so a second adds a
row and routing takes the most specific. `kb.covers(effect)`, `kb.writes(atomicity)`
and `kb.emits(policy)` are keyed by space and REPLACE. `kb.digest()` is a sha256
of the content, order-independent and refused for a space holding a live host
reference. `kb.transaction(term)` runs one term atomically; the body is a term
rather than a callable because `engine_yield/1` cannot unwind through a
transaction, which is the engine's own words for it.

`registerToken(m.engine, /#[0-9a-f]{6}/, (lexeme) => G(...))` extends the
READER: the constructor gets the complete lexeme and the callable never leaves
the host. Needs `library(pcre)`, which `m.engine.capabilities()` reports.

## Reactions, and undoing what already committed

`kb.reacts(pattern, operation, {priority})` declares a rule the ENGINE runs
when a matching atom lands, under the match's bindings; the managed heads are
`insert`, `retract` and `revise`. `kb.agenda(policy)` picks which of several
fires first, from a production system's own conflict-resolution vocabulary:
declaration, recency, specificity, priority, user.

`kb.preAdd(handler)` claims the space's pre-add hook: every write asks the
handler, a definition or a name such as `S.guard`, and does what its verdict
says, `Accept()`, `Accept(atom)`, `Refuse(words)` or `Drop()`.
`kb.postAdd(handler)` reads the same verdicts against the atom that landed.
The claim is made from the space the handler's equations went into. One
handler holds a hook, and a second is refused naming both. The `ScopeHandle`
the door answers undeclares the hook only while its handler still holds it.

`saga(m, receiptSpace)` is the compensating-transaction journal. Declare
`compensates(m, "charge", "refund")`, run steps with `await book.run(term)`,
and `await book.rollback()` undoes them in reverse. A receipt is an ordinary
`(did op args result)` atom. A failed step commits none; rollback preflights
every compensation before undoing anything; a failed compensation keeps its
suffix so a retry resumes. The step is not itself atomic here, because
`engine_yield/1` cannot unwind through a transaction, which leaves the
classical saga [source: Garcia-Molina and Salem, SIGMOD 1987].

## What a definition says about itself

`definitionFacts(m, fn)` lowers a function's body to find out what it reaches
and throws the term away, so nothing is installed. It answers the free names,
the source span, a block comment, the join over the effects the engine
declares, and `unresolved` for the heads it declares none for. `pure` is
conservative: a body reaching an unresolved head is never called pure.

## The command line

```sh
npx tsmetta run program.metta
npx tsmetta eval "(+ 1 2)"
npx tsmetta why "(quad 3)"
npx tsmetta repl
```

## In a browser

`browser/` and `_runtime/` are what a page serves. `metta({ root })` points at
the `_runtime/` directory; a browser fetches three files out of it,
`_runtime/runtime.json` and the two `_runtime/wasm/` assets, and reads the engine and library
sources out of the manifest rather than as files. The documentation site is the
worked example: `website/scripts/bundle-browser.mjs` copies the kit into
`website/public/metta/` and `website/public/metta/worker.js` boots one engine
per page in a Web Worker, which is where a synchronous `run` belongs.

Two things a browser meets that a Node process does not. `loadFile`,
`libraryPath`, `mount` and `lintFile` read host paths and refuse with
`ERR_METTA_UNSUPPORTED`; `run`, `load` and `lint` take source text. And a call
to a door the standard library DECLARES while this build implements nothing for
it answers ITSELF: `!(py-atom "1 + 1")` answers `(py-atom "1 + 1")` where there
is no Python seat. `lint`'s `unimplemented-head` rule names that before it
runs, and it is the rule to run before handing a program to a browser engine.

## Where to read next

- `extensions/node/README.md` is the full surface with worked examples.
- `extensions/node/examples/` are runnable programs.
- The site publishes the same README at `/extensions/node`.
